title: How to Grow an Orange Tree From a Seed
description: Turn a seed you'd normally throw away into a slow-growing houseplant with a little patience.
body: Orange seeds germinate readily, but the tree they grow into is a long-term project. Rinse the pips, soak them overnight, and plant them about 1 cm deep in moist seed compost.
Keep the pot warm and bright and it can sprout within a few weeks. Expect glossy leaves first — fruit, if it ever comes, is years away. Treat it as a beautiful houseplant, not a harvest.

title: Starting Tomato Seeds Indoors
description: A beginner-friendly guide to germinating tomato seeds before the growing season starts.
body: Start tomatoes six to eight weeks before your last frost. Sow seeds about 5 mm deep in damp seed compost, water gently, and keep them at around 20°C.
Once seedlings have two sets of true leaves, pot them on and move them to the brightest spot you have. They need light more than heat to grow sturdy.

title: Can You Grow an Apple Tree From Seed?
description: What actually happens when you plant an apple seed, and how to give it the best chance.
body: An apple seed will sprout, but the tree it grows into won't be the apple you ate. Apples don't come true from seed, so the fruit will be unpredictable.
If you still want to try, chill the seeds in a damp paper towel in the fridge for a few weeks, then plant them. Think of it as an experiment, not an orchard.

title: Preparing Soil for Your First Plant
description: The basics of soil, drainage, and containers before you plant anything.
body: Most houseplants fail because of waterlogged roots, not bad soil. Choose a mix with plenty of air and a pot that has drainage holes.
Fill the pot, firm the soil lightly, and water before planting so it settles. Then water only when the top couple of centimetres feel dry.

title: How Often Should You Really Water Your Plants?
description: Watering schedules depend on plant type, not the calendar. Here's how to read your plant.
body: Forget the calendar and check the soil instead. Push a finger in; if it's dry a few centimetres down, it's time to water.
Water thoroughly until it runs out of the drainage holes, then empty the saucer. Little and often is the fastest way to lose a plant.

title: Indoor Gardening With Little to No Sunlight
description: Apartment living doesn't rule out a green space. Here's what actually survives indoors.
body: Low light doesn't mean no plants. Snake plants, pothos, and ZZ plants tolerate shade and forgive missed waterings.
Rotate them now and then so they grow evenly, and keep them away from cold draughts. A window that faces north can still work.

title: Five Plant Care Habits That Actually Matter
description: Skip the overwhelm — these are the habits that keep most houseplants alive.
body: Five habits do most of the work: water by feel, give the right light, feed lightly in spring and summer, clean the leaves, and repot when roots circle the pot.
None of these is complicated. Consistency matters far more than any special product.

title: What Urban Greening Looks Like on a Balcony
description: You don't need a backyard to make a neighborhood greener.
body: A balcony, a fire escape, or a windowsill is enough to green a street. Even a few pots add shade, food, and a home for pollinators.
Start with tough plants suited to your light and wind, and add more as you learn what thrives in your spot.

title: Kitchen Scraps You Can Regrow This Week
description: From avocado pits to green onion roots — an easy intro to regrowing food.
body: Green onion roots, lettuce bases, celery bottoms, and avocado pits can all be regrown in water or soil with almost no effort.
Keep the water fresh, give them light, and pot them up once roots form. It's the easiest first step into growing your own food.
